claim: 65% of RGCs die within 1 week after optic nerve crush in rats.
source: After optic nerve crush in rats, 65% of RGCs die within 1 week, while less than 1% die after 1 day (Sánchez-Migallón et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sánchez-Migallón et al., 2016.

claim: Less than 1% of RGCs die after 1 day following optic nerve crush in rats.
source: After optic nerve crush in rats, 65% of RGCs die within 1 week, while less than 1% die after 1 day (Sánchez-Migallón et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sánchez-Migallón et al., 2016.

claim: NHS-biotin covalently binds primary amines on proteins, principally lysines and N-terminal amino acids.
source: NHS-biotin covalently binds primary amines on proteins, principally lysines and N-terminal amino acids, adding a biotin group (Figure 1a)
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 1a which shows the chemical reaction, and represents established knowledge about NHS-biotin chemistry.

claim: There was no biotin signal distal to the crush site in injured optic nerves.
source: Notably, there was no biotin signal distal to the crush, confirming the disruption of protein transport and lack of biotin transfer out of axons after injury.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The absence of biotin signal distal to the crush confirms disruption of protein transport after injury.
source: Notably, there was no biotin signal distal to the crush, confirming the disruption of protein transport and lack of biotin transfer out of axons after injury.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observation of no biotin signal distal to the crush site.

claim: 206–300 transported proteins were detected with a range of expression up to 300-fold NSAF values.
source: We detected 206–300 transported proteins with a range of detection of expression up to 300-fold normalized spectral abundance factor (NSAF) values.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data from the experiments.

claim: Pairwise correlation of NSAF values showed high correlation between replicates of both control and crush samples (R = 0.805 and R = 0.914, respectively).
source: To assess reproducibility of the quantitative proteomics in each of these conditions, we used pairwise correlation of NSAF values which showed high correlation between replicates of both control and crush samples (Figure 1d, R = 0.805 and R = 0.914, respectively).
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Total protein content was equivalent in optic nerve crush and control retinas and optic nerves.
source: Total protein content was equivalent in optic nerve crush and control retinas and optic nerves, as expected given the short time between injury and tissue collection (Figure 1e).
evidence: The claim is supported by Ponceau S staining shown in Figure 1e.

claim: Biotinylated protein decreased in the optic nerve after injury compared to control.
source: However, when we compared the biotinylated portion of total protein in crush or control conditions, we found a decrease in axon-transported protein after injury (Figure 1f)
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 1f.

claim: Sncb showed significant decrease in transport into the optic nerve after injury.
source: Sncb and Arf3 but not Gap43 showed significant decreases in transport into the optic nerve after injury (IP + vs. – crush, Figure 2a)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Arf3 showed significant decrease in transport into the optic nerve after injury.
source: Sncb and Arf3 but not Gap43 showed significant decreases in transport into the optic nerve after injury (IP + vs. – crush, Figure 2a)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Gap43 did not show significant decrease in transport into the optic nerve after injury.
source: Sncb and Arf3 but not Gap43 showed significant decreases in transport into the optic nerve after injury (IP + vs. – crush, Figure 2a)
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoprecipitation and western blot data shown in Figure 2a.

claim: The decrease in Sncb transport was significant even when normalizing to the decrease in total transported protein (normalized log2FC = −2.2).
source: and this decrease was significant even when normalizing to the decrease in total transported protein as captured in Figure 1f (normalized log2FC = −2.2 for Sncb, –1.3 for Arf3, n = 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of western blot data.

claim: The decrease in Arf3 transport was significant even when normalizing to the decrease in total transported protein (normalized log2FC = −1.3).
source: and this decrease was significant even when normalizing to the decrease in total transported protein as captured in Figure 1f (normalized log2FC = −2.2 for Sncb, –1.3 for Arf3, n = 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of western blot data.

claim: Transport of Kif5a was significantly decreased after optic nerve crush.
source: In the protein transport ontology, transport of Kif5a, a neuronal kinesin heavy chain motor protein, was significantly decreased.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2b and validated by western blot in Figure 2d-e.

claim: Kif5a is expressed in the mouse retinal ganglion cell layer.
source: We confirmed Kif5a expression is localized to RGCs in the mouse retina using immunohistochemistry (Figure 2c).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Kif5a transport decreased about 2.5-fold relative to the decrease in total axon transport after injury.
source: We normalized biotin-tagged Kif5a to each sample's total biotin-tagged protein (similar to that shown in Figure 1f), and compared injury versus control, which resulted in a significant decrease (about 2.5-fold) in Kif5a transport relative to the decrease in total axon transport after injury (Figure 2e)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative western blot analysis shown in Figure 2e.

claim: Kif5a abundance in the retina was equal with and without injury.
source: Importantly, we saw an equal amount of Kif5a in the retina with and without injury, suggesting that the cause of decreased axon transport is not due to changes in Kif5a abundance in the retina, but in fact reflects a specific anterograde transport deficit.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 2d.

claim: Kif5a is a motor protein in the 45-member kinesin superfamily.
source: Kif5a, the only protein that met both significance and magnitude of change criteria, is a motor protein in the 45-member kinesin superfamily (Hirokawa et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hirokawa et al., 2009.

claim: Kinesin-1 motors are composed of two heavy chain and two light chain proteins.
source: Kinesin-1 motors are composed of two heavy chain and two light chain proteins, where the heavy chains are any of Kif5a, Kif5b, and Kif5c.
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about kinesin-1 motor structure.

claim: Kif5a and Kif5c are neuron-specific kinesin heavy chains.
source: Of these, Kif5a and Kif5c are neuron-specific, and previously described to be expressed in RGCs (Rahman et al., 1999; Butowt and von Bartheld, 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rahman et al., 1999 and Butowt and von Bartheld, 2007.

claim: Kif5b transport did not change in relative transport after optic nerve injury.
source: First, another kinesin heavy chain, Kif5b, did not change in relative transport after injury, suggesting specificity in kinesin isoform transport failure.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: Transport of Klc1 was not reduced to the same extent as Kif5a after injury.
source: Second, transport of Klc1, a light chain partner of the heavy chain Kif5a, also was not reduced to the same extent as Kif5a.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a.

claim: No significant change in transport of both dynein subunits was discovered after optic nerve injury.
source: We did not discover any significant change in transport of both dynein subunits identified in our transportome, although more work may be needed to explore this question.
evidence: The claim is supported by mass spectrometry data analysis.

claim: Kif5a synthesis decreased in the retina 3 weeks after induction of glaucoma.
source: Among these, Kif5a showed decreased synthesis when normalized to the total newly synthesized proteome after induction of glaucoma, while Kif5b was relatively unchanged (Figure 2g, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b, complete data in ).
evidence: The claim is supported by BONCAT and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Kif5b synthesis was relatively unchanged 3 weeks after induction of glaucoma.
source: Among these, Kif5a showed decreased synthesis when normalized to the total newly synthesized proteome after induction of glaucoma, while Kif5b was relatively unchanged (Figure 2g, Figure 2—figure supplement 1b, complete data in ).
evidence: The claim is supported by BONCAT and mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2g.

claim: Kif5a is enriched in the amacrine cell/RGC cluster of cells compared to other retinal cell types in both mouse and human retinas.
source: We found that Kif5a was enriched in the amacrine cell/RGC cluster of cells compared to other retinal cell types in both mouse and human, whereas Kif5b was expressed more ubiquitously across retinal cell types (Figure 3c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3c-d.

claim: Kif5b is expressed more ubiquitously across retinal cell types in both mouse and human retinas.
source: We found that Kif5a was enriched in the amacrine cell/RGC cluster of cells compared to other retinal cell types in both mouse and human, whereas Kif5b was expressed more ubiquitously across retinal cell types (Figure 3c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by single-cell RNA sequencing data shown in Figure 3c-d.

claim: There was almost a complete loss of Kif5a in the retina one month after AAV-cre injection in Kif5a floxed mice.
source: One month after injection, there was almost a complete loss of Kif5a in the retina, and a complete loss in the optic nerve, with neither loss nor compensatory upregulation of Kif5c (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: There was a complete loss of Kif5a in the optic nerve one month after AAV-cre injection in Kif5a floxed mice.
source: One month after injection, there was almost a complete loss of Kif5a in the retina, and a complete loss in the optic nerve, with neither loss nor compensatory upregulation of Kif5c (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: There was neither loss nor compensatory upregulation of Kif5c after Kif5a knockout.
source: One month after injection, there was almost a complete loss of Kif5a in the retina, and a complete loss in the optic nerve, with neither loss nor compensatory upregulation of Kif5c (Figure 4a).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Bin1 was identified as an Alzheimer's disease locus through GWAS studies.
source: Bin1, for example, was identified as an Alzheimer's disease locus through GWAS studies (Seshadri et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Seshadri et al., 2010.

claim: Bin1 localizes to the axon initial segment and nodes of Ranvier.
source: and localizes to the axon initial segment and nodes of Ranvier acting downstream of c-myc, an injury-response transcription factor in RGCs (Belin et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Belin et al., 2015.

claim: Sh3gl2 is enriched in synaptic terminals.
source: Sh3gl2, also known as endophilin A1, is enriched in synaptic terminals and interacts with synaptic proteins such as synaptojanin and regulates clathrin-mediated synaptic endocytosis (Milosevic et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Milosevic et al., 2011.

claim: Sh3gl2 interacts with synaptic proteins such as synaptojanin.
source: Sh3gl2, also known as endophilin A1, is enriched in synaptic terminals and interacts with synaptic proteins such as synaptojanin and regulates clathrin-mediated synaptic endocytosis (Milosevic et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Milosevic et al., 2011.

claim: Sh3gl2 regulates clathrin-mediated synaptic endocytosis.
source: Sh3gl2, also known as endophilin A1, is enriched in synaptic terminals and interacts with synaptic proteins such as synaptojanin and regulates clathrin-mediated synaptic endocytosis (Milosevic et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Milosevic et al., 2011.

claim: Mitochondrial-associated genes are significantly over-represented among proteins that decrease in transport in both optic nerve crush and Kif5a knockout.
source: Using Gene Ontology to cluster all proteins that decrease in transport in both optic nerve crush and Kif5a knockout, we discovered a significantly over-represented number of mitochondrial-associated genes in common (Figure 5a–b).
evidence: The claim is supported by Gene Ontology analysis shown in Figure 5a-b.

claim: AAV2-mediated Kif5a knockdown significantly reduced the average velocity of non-stationary mitochondria compared to an AAV2 scrambled shRNA virus.
source: AAV2-mediated Kif5a knockdown significantly reduced the average velocity of non-stationary mitochondria compared to an AAV2 scrambled shRNA virus, as shown in kymographs of mitochondrial transport (Figure 5c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 5c-d.

claim: Kif5a knockdown resulted in a significant reduction in anterograde mitochondrial transport.
source: By quantifying the number of mitochondria transported in each direction, we found a significant reduction in anterograde transport (Figure 5e).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of mitochondrial transport shown in Figure 5e.

claim: Primary RGCs treated with an AAV2 Kif5a expression virus demonstrated significantly increased average mitochondrial velocity.
source: Primary RGCs treated with an AAV2 Kif5a expression virus demonstrated significantly increased average velocity (Figure 5f–g).
evidence: The claim is supported by live cell imaging data shown in Figure 5f-g.

claim: Kif5a overexpression resulted in a significant increase in the fraction of anterogradely moving mitochondria compared to control.
source: We also found a significant increase in the fraction of anterogradely moving mitochondria compared to control (Figure 5h).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of mitochondrial transport shown in Figure 5h.

claim: Kif5a expression is necessary for anterograde mitochondrial transport in mammalian RGCs.
source: Thus Kif5a expression is necessary for and can promote anterograde mitochondrial transport in mammalian RGCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the knockdown and overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Kif5a can promote anterograde mitochondrial transport in mammalian RGCs.
source: Thus Kif5a expression is necessary for and can promote anterograde mitochondrial transport in mammalian RGCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the knockdown and overexpression experiments shown in Figure 5.

claim: Kif5a associates with several members of the HnRNP family, including HnRNPA1.
source: Kif5a associates with several members of the HnRNP family, including HnRNPA1 (Kanai et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kanai et al., 2004.

claim: HnRNPA1 has been shown to play a role in concentration-dependent stress granule formation in other neurodegenerative diseases including ALS.
source: HnRNPA1 has been shown to play a role in concentration-dependent stress granule formation in other neurodegenerative diseases including ALS (Kim et al., 2013; Molliex et al., 2015; Deshaies et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Kim et al., 2013; Molliex et al., 2015; Deshaies et al., 2018.

claim: HnRNPA1 knockdown significantly decreased RGC survival after optic nerve injury.
source: HnRNPA1 knockdown significantly decreased RGC survival after injury (Figure 5i–j).
evidence: The claim is supported by RGC quantification data shown in Figure 5i-j.

claim: RGC density did not change 1 month after Kif5b homozygous knockout.
source: RGC density did not change 1 month after Kif5b homozygous knockout (Figure 6—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by RGC quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: A significant 44% decrease in RGC survival was detected 1 month after Kif5a homozygous knockout.
source: but we detected a significant 44% decrease in RGC survival 1 month after Kif5a homozygous knockout.
evidence: The claim is supported by RGC quantification data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Kif5a-dependent RGC death led to significant optic nerve atrophy.
source: This Kif5a-dependent RGC death also led to significant optic nerve atrophy, confirming axonal degeneration in addition to RGC death (Figure 6b).
evidence: The claim is supported by optic nerve diameter measurements shown in Figure 6b.

claim: A significant decrease of 22% RGC survival was found in heterozygous Kif5a knockout mice, about half of the cell death seen in the homozygous Kif5a knockout.
source: We assayed gene dose dependency using a heterozygous Kif5afl/+ mouse line with AAV-cre and found a significant decrease of 22% RGC survival, about half of the cell death seen in the homozygous Kif5a knockout (Figure 6c; 1-2).
evidence: The claim is supported by RGC quantification data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: An almost complete loss of RGCs was observed 4 months after Kif5a knockout.
source: To determine if only 44% of RGCs are susceptible to cell death or if Kif5a loss results in progressive degeneration, we aged a cohort of mice to 4 months after knockout and observed an almost complete loss of RGCs (Figure 6c; 3-4).
evidence: The claim is supported by RGC quantification data shown in Figure 6c.

claim: Visual responses were almost completely lost 6 months after Kif5a knockout, quantified by P50 to N95 amplitude.
source: To test whether this effect could be a downregulation of Brn3a, we also measured pattern electroretinograms for function of RGCs. Visual responses were almost completely lost 6 months after knockout, quantified by P50 to N95 amplitude (Figure 6d).
evidence: The claim is supported by pattern electroretinogram data shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Loss of Kif5a induces a progressive neurodegeneration of RGCs.
source: These data indicate that the loss of a specific motor protein Kif5a, but not Kif5b, induces a progressive neurodegeneration as well as a dose-dependent neurodegeneration of RGCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the time course data showing increasing RGC loss over time after Kif5a knockout.

claim: Loss of Kif5a induces a dose-dependent neurodegeneration of RGCs.
source: These data indicate that the loss of a specific motor protein Kif5a, but not Kif5b, induces a progressive neurodegeneration as well as a dose-dependent neurodegeneration of RGCs.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the heterozygous vs homozygous knockout data showing gene dose dependency.

claim: There were no changes in RGC cell death 1 month post viral injection of Kif5a overexpression without injury.
source: Interestingly, while there were no changes in cell death 1 month post viral injection without injury (Figure 7b)
evidence: The claim is supported by RGC quantification data shown in Figure 7b.

claim: There was a 33% decrease in RGC survival after optic nerve crush with Kif5a overexpression compared to control.
source: there was a 33% decrease in RGC survival after optic nerve crush with Kif5a overexpression compared to control (Figure 7c–d).
evidence: The claim is supported by RGC quantification data shown in Figure 7c-d.

claim: Maintaining physiological levels of Kif5a transport is crucial for RGC survival after injury.
source: Therefore, maintaining physiological levels of Kif5a transport—and not above or below this level—is crucial for RGC survival after injury.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the finding that both loss and overexpression of Kif5a are detrimental to RGC survival after injury.

claim: Axon transport failure has been pathophysiologically linked to RGC death in glaucoma.
source: Axon transport failure has been pathophysiologically linked to RGC death in glaucoma, as well as to other neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and Alzheimer's disease (Zhang et al., 2004; Nicolas et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2004 and Nicolas et al., 2018.

claim: Axon transport failure has been pathophysiologically linked to ALS.
source: Axon transport failure has been pathophysiologically linked to RGC death in glaucoma, as well as to other neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and Alzheimer's disease (Zhang et al., 2004; Nicolas et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2004 and Nicolas et al., 2018.

claim: Axon transport failure has been pathophysiologically linked to Alzheimer's disease.
source: Axon transport failure has been pathophysiologically linked to RGC death in glaucoma, as well as to other neurodegenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and Alzheimer's disease (Zhang et al., 2004; Nicolas et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Zhang et al., 2004 and Nicolas et al., 2018.

claim: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A can be caused by mutations in Kif1b.
source: Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 2A can be caused by mutations in Kif1b (Zhao et al., 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Zhao et al., 2001.

claim: Congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles can be caused by mutations in Kif21a.
source: congenital fibrosis of the extraocular muscles can be caused by mutations in Kif21a
evidence: The claim is supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: A loss-of-function mutation in Kif5a motor domain can result in hereditary spastic paraplegia.
source: and a loss-of-function mutation in Kif5a motor domain can result in hereditary spastic paraplegia (Reid et al., 2002; Xia et al., 2003; Tessa et al., 2008; Morfini et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Reid et al., 2002; Xia et al., 2003; Tessa et al., 2008; Morfini et al., 2009.

claim: Different loss-of-function mutations in Kif5a, all affecting the cargo binding domain, are causative in some cases of ALS.
source: Different loss-of-function mutations in Kif5a, all affecting the cargo binding domain, are causative in some cases of ALS (Brenner et al., 2018; Nicolas et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Brenner et al., 2018 and Nicolas et al., 2018.

claim: Several synaptic proteins such as Snap25, synaptotagmin, and syntaxin 1a have been identified as cargoes of the Kif5 family.
source: Through IP and immunoisolation assays, several synaptic proteins such as Snap25, synaptotagmin, and syntaxin 1a have been identified as cargoes of the Kif5 family (Toda et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Toda et al., 2008.

claim: GABARAP has been shown to be specific to Kif5a.
source: but only a few proteins have been shown to be specific to Kif5a, such as GABARAP (Nakajima et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nakajima et al., 2012.

claim: Kif5 motors regulate mitochondrial trafficking in Drosophila through the adaptor proteins Milton and Miro.
source: Kif5 motors regulate mitochondrial trafficking in Drosophila and mammalian hippocampal neurons through the adaptor proteins Milton and Miro (Glater et al., 2006; Macaskill et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Glater et al., 2006 and Macaskill et al., 2009.

claim: Kif5 motors regulate mitochondrial trafficking in mammalian hippocampal neurons through the adaptor proteins Milton and Miro.
source: Kif5 motors regulate mitochondrial trafficking in Drosophila and mammalian hippocampal neurons through the adaptor proteins Milton and Miro (Glater et al., 2006; Macaskill et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Glater et al., 2006 and Macaskill et al., 2009.

claim: Mitochondria localize to injured axons during the normal course of regeneration in C. elegans.
source: In Caenorhabditis elegans, mitochondria localize to injured axons during the normal course of regeneration (Han et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Han et al., 2016.

claim: Manipulating mitochondrial mobilization through overexpression of Armcx1 produces survival and regenerative effects in mammalian RGCs.
source: In non-regenerating neurons, like mammalian RGCs, manipulating mitochondrial mobilization through overexpression of Armcx1 produces a similar survival and regenerative effect (Cartoni et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cartoni et al., 2016.

claim: Kif5a may regulate mitochondrial transport in zebrafish.
source: Previous studies have shown that Kif5a may regulate mitochondrial transport in zebrafish (Campbell et al., 2014)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Campbell et al., 2014.

claim: Kif5a may regulate mitochondrial transport in cultured hippocampal neurons.
source: and cultured hippocampal neurons (Chen and Sheng, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chen and Sheng, 2013.

claim: Regulation of kinesin transport depends on phosphorylation states.
source: Regulation of kinesin transport is known to depend on phosphorylation states (Morfini et al., 2001)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Morfini et al., 2001.

claim: Regulation of kinesin transport depends on calcium-dependent inhibition by mitochondrial cargo.
source: calcium-dependent inhibition by mitochondrial cargo (Wang and Schwarz, 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang and Schwarz, 2009.

claim: Regulation of kinesin transport depends on conformational state changes by kinesin light chains.
source: conformational state changes by kinesin light chains
evidence: The claim represents established knowledge about kinesin regulation.

claim: Regulation of kinesin transport depends on inhibition by MAP2 at the axon initial segment.
source: inhibition by MAP2 at the axon initial segment (Gumy et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Gumy et al., 2017.

claim: Regulation of kinesin transport depends on autoinhibition of the motor domain by inactive kinesin heavy chains.
source: and autoinhibition of the motor domain by inactive kinesin heavy chains (Cai et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Cai et al., 2007.

claim: Removing autoinhibitory domains or truncation of the motor beyond the first coiled-coil domain creates constitutively active kinesins.
source: Removing autoinhibitory domains or truncation of the motor beyond the first coiled-coil domain creates constitutively active kinesins, potentially circumventing any inherent axonal inhibition (Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2016.
